newsitem.title: MEXICO: New Mexican rebels threaten to step up attacks.
newsitem.headline: New Mexican rebels threaten to step up attacks.

text.p: A recently emerged Mexican guerrilla group, the Popular Revolutionary Army (EPR), will step up attacks on government forces if it sees military repression getting worse, a rebel leader warned.

Speaking to reporters at a clandestine news conference in the southern state of Oaxaca on Friday, an EPR commander with the nom de guerre Francisco said rebel units were actively preparing for combat in different parts of the country.
A partial text of his comments was obtained by Reuters.

"There is a worsening of repression and if it intensifies more than it has already, we will have to respond differently," said Francisco, who described himself as a member of the EPR's national high command.
"This level (of combat) will have to pass to another level, a higher level of confrontation."

Flanked by what reporters said were about 60 armed guards, their faces covered with bandanas and wearing the EPR's khaki and coffee-coloured uniforms, Francisco presided over the meeting at a table roughly assembled from a fallen tree. Logs were used as seats, reporters said.

The meeting, held in wooded hills seven hours by road and three hours by foot from the state capital, marked the first major EPR media event since it launched attacks on police and military posts in various Mexican states on Aug. 28.

According to Radio Red, Francisco claimed the rebels killed 41 officials and wounded 48 during the coordinated assaults. The government said 15 died and 22 were wounded in the fighting, including three rebels.

In a report on the EPR meeting, the radio station quoted Francisco as saying the EPR may be forced to disperse its forces if government troops continue their crackdown in the South. Those comments could not be immediately confirmed.

Francisco said the rebel force is carrying out military actions according to what he called a "campaign of self-defence." That is, it has not officially waged war on the government, but it threatens to strike if provoked.

Thousands of government troops have poured into southern and eastern Mexico, where the movement is believed to have its roots, since the masked guerrillas announced their existence at a political rally on June 28 in neighbouring Guerrero state.
But the EPR has remained largely elusive, carrying out classic guerrilla-style hit and run attacks, distributing propaganda and mocking the government via communiques.

Francisco said it has troops at the ready who have not yet taken part in acts of combat. "Currently there are EPR units that are preparing for combat in various parts of the country," he said, without being more specific.
His comments come amid fears that the EPR would disrupt Independence Day celebrations in Mexico on Sunday and Monday.

Those fears were stoked by the discovery of a small bomb in Mexico's Monument to the Revolution on Friday. It was not clear who planted it. The EPR has denied planning attacks on civilians during the celebrations.

Seperately, Radio Red said EPR gunmen appeared for the first time in San Luis Potosi, capital of the state of the same name in eastern Mexico, on Saturday. They left leaflets in a shoe box and hung up an EPR banner that remained for three hours before police tore it down.

In the capital, Mayor Oscar Espinosa told reporters security had been stepped up following the discovery of the bomb ahead of Sunday's celebrations when tens of thousands are expected to gather in the main square to hear President Ernesto Zedillo give the traditional "Cry of Independence".
